P.claim: COVID-19 pandemic pre-planned with the help from Bill Gates.
P.justification: The claim that the COVID-19 pandemic was pre-planned with Bill Gates's involvement is unfounded, as no documented evidence—such as meeting minutes, communications, or financial records—supports a conspiracy to create and release SARS-CoV-2, and [the scientific consensus points to a natural zoonotic origin](https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/mammalia-2020-0044/html?lang=en). While the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation partnered with the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security and the World Economic Forum on the [Event 201 pandemic simulation](https://fullfact.org/health/event-201-coronavirus-pandemic/) in October 2019, organizers explicitly stated it "was not a prediction" of COVID-19. [Fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked](https://factcheck.afp.com/bill-gates-bogeyman-virus-conspiracy-theorists) claims that Gates funded the virus's creation, noting that the foundation's substantial investments in vaccine development and global health initiatives, including [pre-funding candidate COVID-19 vaccines](https://nymag.com/intelligencer/2020/09/bill-gates-hopes-covid-19-pandemic-doesnt-stretch-past-2022-interview.html), were philanthropic in nature. Gates's pre-pandemic warnings about infectious disease risks, such as his [2015 TED Talk](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/05/12/bill-gates-wishes-hed-done-more-to-warn-about-pandemic-danger.html), align with longstanding general risk assessments by epidemiologists rather than indicating prior specific knowledge of COVID-19. No law enforcement or intelligence agency has found evidence supporting the conspiracy, [no whistleblowers have corroborated it](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/08/25/fact-check-plandemic-sequel-makes-false-claims-bill-gates/5627223002/), and [National Geographic](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/coronavirus-origins-misinformation-yan-report-fact-check-cvd) has documented how misinformation about the virus's origins has been systematically debunked.
P.judge_reasoning:
## Step 1: Summary of Key Findings

The extensive fact-check found **no credible evidence** supporting the claim that the COVID-19 pandemic was pre-planned with Bill Gates's involvement. Specifically: there are no documented records of any conspiracy to create and release SARS-CoV-2; no evidence that the Gates Foundation funded research resulting in the virus's creation; the scientific consensus points to a zoonotic origin, not deliberate engineering; the Event 201 simulation exercise (which the Gates Foundation helped fund) was explicitly stated not to be a prediction and is consistent with standard pandemic preparedness; no law enforcement or intelligence agency has concluded the pandemic was pre-planned; no whistleblowers have corroborated such claims; and Gates's public pandemic warnings align with longstanding general epidemiological risk assessments rather than prior specific knowledge. Multiple independent fact-checking organizations (AFP, USA Today, Full Fact) have characterized these allegations as baseless conspiracy theories.

## Step 2: Additional Information Needed

The evidence is comprehensive and consistent across multiple independent sources. No further investigation is required to reach a clear conclusion.

## Step 3: Conclusion

The claim that the COVID-19 pandemic was "pre-planned with the help from Bill Gates" is a conspiracy theory that is entirely unsupported by any documented evidence. Every avenue of inquiry—scientific origins, financial records, intelligence assessments, whistleblowers, and Gates's own documented activities—fails to provide any corroboration, while multiple credible fact-checking organizations and the scientific consensus explicitly contradict the claim. The decision is `refuted`.

Epidemiologically, COVID-19 spread extensively in regions with [no 5G infrastructure](https://theconversation.com/conspiracy-theories-about-5g-networks-have-skyrocketed-since-covid-19-139374), such as Iran, contradicting what would be predicted if 5G were the cause. Any observed statistical correlations between 5G coverage and case counts are explained by confounding factors like population density. The claim originated from [pre-existing anti-technology conspiracy theories amplified on social media](https://allianceforscience.org/blog/2020/04/5g-whats-behind-the-latest-covid-conspiracy-theory/) and has been unanimously debunked by [independent fact-checkers and health authorities](https://www.ucc.org/daily_covid_19_brief_issue_62/).
P.judge_reasoning:
The recorded evidence comprehensively refutes the claim. Key findings include: the scientific consensus from the WHO and other bodies states that 5G radio frequencies within safety guidelines have no established health effects; COVID-19 is definitively caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus; 5G uses non-ionizing radiation which cannot cause viral infections; the disease spread extensively in regions without 5G networks; and independent fact-checkers have consistently labeled the claim false. No scientific mechanism links 5G to the creation or causation of COVID-19.

The evidence is clear and consistent across multiple domains—biology, epidemiology, and expert consensus. No further investigation is needed to finalize the fact-check.

Based on the overwhelming evidence that directly and explicitly contradicts the claim, my conclusion is that the claim is false.

`refuted`

Scientific consensus asserts that herd immunity against COVID-19 cannot be safely or reliably achieved without widespread vaccination, labeling the idea of achieving it through natural infection a "dangerous fallacy." The evidence shows that vaccines are considered a far safer and more effective method than deliberate exposure, and no credible medical or scientific authorities endorse the practice described in the claim. P.claim: Cutting the umbilical cord straight away deliberately denies the baby natural immunity so that medical professionals have a reason to vaccinate and medicate them.

Evidence shows delayed clamping does not significantly improve immune function or reduce infections ([PMC6408182](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6408182/)), and experts characterize immediate clamping as a legacy practice being updated based on science, not a conspiracy to promote vaccines ([americanpregnancy.org](https://americanpregnancy.org/healthy-pregnancy/labor-and-birth/delayed-cord-clamping/)). Vaccination schedules are standardized independently of cord clamping ([JAMA](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2706137/created)).
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the fact-check, the evidence shows that while early umbilical cord clamping was historically a common clinical practice, it is not medically supported and is being replaced by guidelines recommending delayed clamping (30–60 seconds) due to benefits like increased blood volume and iron stores. However, the transferred placental blood primarily contains red blood cells and stem cells, and studies found no effect on sepsis or infection rates, contradicting the claim that it provides critical "natural immunity." Vaccination schedules are standardized independently of cord management, and experts attribute early clamping to legacy practices, not a deliberate conspiracy to promote vaccination.

The evidence is clear and comprehensive, covering medical guidelines, clinical practice, the physiological effects of cord clamping, expert opinions, and the lack of any historical or legal records supporting the claim's implied intent. No further investigation is required to evaluate the claim.

The claim that immediate cord clamping is a deliberate act to deny natural immunity to justify vaccination is refuted by the evidence. Medical practice is shifting toward delayed clamping based on infant health benefits, not a coordinated effort, and there is no link between clamping timing and vaccination necessity. Therefore, the claim is `refuted`.

P.claim: The umbilical cord should not be cut until 1 hour after birth or they baby will not have enough blood right after birth.
P.justification: The claim exaggerates both the recommended timing and the consequences of cord clamping. Major health organizations, including [ACOG](https://www.acog.org/news/news-releases/2016/12/acog-recommends-delayed-umbilical-cord-clamping-for-all-healthy-infants) and the [WHO](https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance/browse-all-guidance/scientific-impact-papers/clamping-of-the-umbilical-cord-and-placental-transfusion-scientific-impact-paper-no-14), recommend delaying cord clamping for **30 to 60 seconds** (or up to 1–3 minutes), not one hour, as this is sufficient to allow meaningful placental transfusion—research shows that umbilical blood flow typically ceases by approximately [140 seconds after birth](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4687772/), making an hour-long delay unnecessary. While delayed clamping does increase hemoglobin levels and improve iron stores, as supported by [ACOG's evidence review](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/experts-and-stories/ask-acog/what-is-delayed-cord-clamping), no recognized guideline or clinical trial recommends waiting a full hour, and no studies have evaluated the safety or outcomes of such an extended delay. Furthermore, the claim's assertion that a baby "will not have enough blood" without an hour-long wait is misleading; the [research](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fped.2019.00405) indicates that the standard 30–60 second delay is sufficient for adequate placental transfusion, and immediate clamping may only be necessary in specific emergencies such as [neonatal asphyxia requiring resuscitation](https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance/browse-all-guidance/scientific-impact-papers/clamping-of-the-umbilical-cord-and-placental-transfusion-scientific-impact-paper-no-14).
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the fact-check reveals that while delayed cord clamping is supported by major health organizations (e.g., ACOG, WHO) for benefits like increased blood volume and iron stores, the recommended delay is 30–60 seconds or up to 1–3 minutes—not one hour. The evidence shows placental transfusion typically ceases around 140 seconds after birth, and no guidelines or robust studies recommend or support a one-hour delay. Additionally, the claim that the baby "will not have enough blood right after birth" if clamped earlier is overstated; immediate clamping can reduce cardiac output, but a delay of 1–3 minutes is sufficient to improve blood volume and hemodynamic stability.

The conclusion is that the claim is not supported by the evidence and is refuted by established medical guidelines.

`refuted`

P.claim: 99% of people recover from COVID-19.

P.judge_reasoning:
The fact-check reveals that the "99% recovery" claim, originating from a 2020 blog post, lacks a clear, consistent definition of "recovery." Available evidence contradicts this figure: a peer-reviewed study found a case-recovery rate of 46% in Europe, and aggregated global data from health agencies shows recovery rates varying widely by country, with none reaching 99%. Furthermore, clinical definitions of "recovery" (e.g., from the CDC) are narrow and do not account for persistent symptoms like Long COVID, which affects a significant portion of patients.

Based on the recorded evidence, the claim is clearly contradicted by data showing substantially lower recovery rates and by the problematic, narrow definition of "recovery" it would require to be true. Therefore, the final decision is `refuted`.

P.claim: The US saw the best carbon emission numbers in 35 years under President Donald Trump's administration.
P.justification: The fact-check concludes the claim is REFUTED, finding that while U.S. emissions did decline during the Trump administration, the pace of reduction slowed compared to the previous decade, with only a 0.5% cumulative decrease in CO₂ emissions over 2017–2019. The lowest emissions year, 2019, represented a 27-year low, not a 35-year one, and the decline was primarily driven by long-term market shifts—from coal to natural gas and renewables—rather than new federal climate policies, which experts note were lacking. Additionally, the temporary drop in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic does not validate the claim, and overall trends during this period are seen as a fluctuation within the long-term climate challenge.
P.judge_reasoning:
**Summary of Key Insights:**  
The fact-check reveals that U.S. carbon emissions were already on a downward trend before Donald Trump took office in 2017, with a 14% reduction from 2005 to 2016. During Trump's presidency (2017-2020), emissions continued to decline but at a slower pace—only 0.5% cumulative from 2017 to 2019, compared to an 11% drop under Obama. The lowest point during this period was in 2019, which marked a 27-year low (since 1992), not a 35-year low. This decline was primarily driven by market forces such as the shift from coal to natural gas and renewables, while federal policies like repealing the Clean Power Plan were projected to increase emissions. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a sharp drop in 2020, but even excluding that year, the claim of "best" numbers in 35 years is unsupported. Experts attribute the slowdown to a lack of new climate policy and view the trends as temporary fluctuations.

**Lacking Information:**  
No significant information gaps remain; the evidence clearly addresses the claim's timeframe, emission metrics, comparisons to previous administrations, and influencing factors.

**Conclusion:**  
Based on the recorded evidence, the claim that "the US saw the best carbon emission numbers in 35 years under President Donald Trump's administration" is refuted because the lowest emissions occurred in 2019 as a 27-year low, not a 35-year low, and the decline was slower than in prior administrations, driven by market dynamics rather than policy improvements. Therefore, the decision is `refuted`.

Ferdinand Marcos was a 26-year-old lawyer in 1944 with no governmental or diplomatic position, and the Philippines was a U.S. commonwealth not yet independent. Official founding documents and reputable historical sources do not list either individual as a signatory, founder, or negotiating team member for these institutions.

The evidence is clear and comprehensive, leaving no reasonable doubt about the claim's validity.

The claim that President Ferdinand Marcos and Dr. Jose Rizal established and founded the World Bank and International Monetary Fund is directly and conclusively refuted by the historical record. Dr. Rizal's death in 1896 predates the institutions' creation by nearly half a century, and Ferdinand Marcos held no relevant position in 1944 to participate in their founding. Therefore, the claim is `refuted`.

While one early observational study noted a correlation, large-scale subsequent research, including a [meta-analysis of over one million participants](https://pesquisa.bvsalud.org/global-literature-on-novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov/resource/pt/covidwho-1889175), found that flu vaccination was actually associated with a *reduced* risk of COVID-19 infection. For President Trump specifically, his documented flu shots were not a factor; his contraction of COVID-19 in October 2020 is attributed to [exposure at crowded, close-contact events](https://news.yahoo.com/as-covid-spread-through-white-house-top-trump-allies-and-family-members-mingled-at-events-in-dc-213300887.html) and his [age and health profile](https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/pharmacy/8-drugs-trump-has-been-given-for-his-covid-19-treatment.html), not prior vaccination. Health misinformation watchdogs like [FactCheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2020/04/no-evidence-that-flu-shot-increases-risk-of-covid-19/) have categorized this claim as false.
P.judge_reasoning:
### Summary of Key Insights
The fact-check reveals that there is no peer-reviewed evidence establishing a causal mechanism by which flu vaccines increase susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection; major health organizations like the WHO and CDC confirm no such link exists. Observational studies that noted correlations are confounded and not considered proof of causation, while systematic reviews and meta-analyses indicate that flu vaccination is associated with a reduced risk of COVID-19 infection or no increased risk. For President Donald Trump, his documented flu vaccination history and multiple potential exposure events to SARS-CoV-2, along with alternative factors like age and health status, were identified, and the claim has been flagged as false by health misinformation monitors.

### Information Lacking
The evidence is comprehensive and aligns against the claim, so no further investigation is required to finalize the fact-check.

### Conclusion
Based on the recorded evidence, including the absence of a causal mechanism, consensus from public health organizations, and large-scale studies refuting any increased susceptibility, the claim that previous flu vaccines made President Donald Trump susceptible to COVID-19 is not supported and is explicitly contradicted. Therefore, the decision is `refuted`.

The **New York Supreme Court** settlement required **Donald Trump** to pay $2 million and dissolved the **Trump Foundation**, but no admission of guilt was made, and the children were not found to have "stolen" donations for personal use; instead, funds raised for **St. Jude's Children's Research Hospital** were misdirected through inflated expenses at Trump Organization golf courses.

Specifically, the New York court's resolution did not impose a permanent ban on any of them; instead, Donald Trump and his children were subject to stipulations such as attending board training. Furthermore, the evidence only confirms a direct legal restriction against Eric Trump from operating a charity in one context, not a universal, permanent ban applying to all three individuals as stated in the claim. There was no admission of guilt in the settlement.

The recorded evidence is sufficient to assess the claim against the provided decision options, so no further investigation is required.

Based on the findings, the claim that the three individuals are permanently banned from operating any charity is not supported by the legal settlement, which did not impose such a universal and perpetual prohibition. Therefore, the claim is `refuted`.

P.claim: Someone who couldn't afford health care under Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act gets penalized $10,000
P.justification: The fact-check refutes the claim by showing the Affordable Care Act's penalty was nowhere near $10,000. The penalty was calculated as the greater of a flat fee (e.g., $695 per adult) or a percentage of income (up to 2.5%), and was legally capped at the national average premium for a bronze-level health plan (e.g., $2,484 for 2015) ([CRS Report](https://sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/R41331.pdf)). Furthermore, individuals who could not afford insurance were exempt from the penalty altogether ([Healthcare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/coverage/preventive-care-benefits/)). Official data from the IRS and analyses from agencies like the [CBO](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/43628) confirm actual penalties were hundreds of dollars, not thousands ([KFF Penalty Calculator](https://www.kff.org/interactive/penalty-calculator/)).
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the fact-check reveals that the Affordable Care Act (ACA) did impose a tax penalty for lacking health insurance, but the penalty amount was significantly lower than $10,000 and was capped at the national average premium for a bronze-level plan (e.g., $2,484 for a single individual in 2015). Furthermore, the ACA included an affordability exemption, meaning individuals who could not afford coverage (where the cost exceeded approximately 8% of household income) were exempt from the penalty entirely.

The evidence is clear and comprehensive, showing that the claim's assertion of a $10,000 penalty for someone who couldn't afford care is incorrect on both the penalty amount and the existence of the affordability exemption. No further investigation is required.

Therefore, the claim is explicitly and clearly refuted by the evidence. `refuted`

No information is lacking to finalize the fact-check; the evidence clearly distinguishes between the two entities.

The claim incorrectly conflates Hunter Biden's role in a supporting nonprofit with the leadership of the Nobel Prize-winning UN agency. Therefore, the claim is false.

`refuted`

**Summary of Key Insights**  
The fact-check confirms that a 2008 paper co-authored by Dr. Anthony Fauci concluded bacterial pneumonia was the predominant cause of death during the 1918 influenza pandemic, primarily due to secondary bacterial infections following influenza virus infection. However, the paper does not mention masks, face coverings, or respiratory protection as a factor in these deaths, and the scientific consensus on the pandemic's lethality does not link mask use to bacterial pneumonia.

**Missing Information**  
No further investigation is required, as the evidence clearly addresses the claim's assertions about the paper's content.

**Conclusion**  
The claim states that Dr. Fauci's 2008 paper attributed most 1918 pandemic deaths to bacterial pneumonia caused by wearing masks. The evidence shows that while the paper does identify bacterial pneumonia as the primary cause of death, it contains no discussion of masks or any mechanism linking mask use to pneumonia. The claim therefore introduces an unsupported causal link not present in the source material. `refuted`

P.claim: A third of excess deaths in the United States between 1 March and  1 August 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic could not be directly attributed to the coronavirus
P.justification: According to [a JAMA study](https://www.cnn.com/2020/10/12/health/us-deaths-covid-19-pandemic-jama-study/index.html), there were approximately 225,530 excess deaths in the United States between March 1 and August 1, 2020, of which 150,541 — roughly 67% — had COVID-19 listed as an underlying or contributing cause of death on death certificates, leaving approximately one-third of excess deaths not directly attributed to the coronavirus. This is consistent with the claim, though [a separate study by Andrew Stokes et al.](https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/US-covid-deaths-may-be-underestimated-36-percent) found a slightly lower proportion of 26% non-COVID-attributed excess deaths over a different but overlapping period (February 1 – September 23, 2020). The Stokes study noted that the excess mortality framework inherently captures deaths where COVID-19 may have been misclassified or undiagnosed, as well as indirect pandemic-related deaths. The [National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS)](https://theconversation.com/279-700-extra-deaths-in-the-us-so-far-in-this-pandemic-year-147887) provides the underlying death data, with the CDC using a statistical model based on the previous three years of mortality data to calculate expected baseline deaths. Overall, the evidence supports the claim's figure, as the JAMA data directly shows that about a third of excess deaths in the specified period lacked a COVID-19 attribution on death certificates.
P.judge_reasoning:
**Step 1: Summary of key findings**

The fact-check reveals a tension in the evidence. On one hand, the JAMA study reported by CNN found 225,530 excess deaths in the U.S. between March 1 and August 1, 2020, of which 150,541 (67%) had COVID-19 listed as an underlying or contributing cause of death — meaning roughly 33%, or about a third, were *not* directly attributed to COVID-19, which aligns with the claim. The Stokes et al. study found a similar but somewhat lower figure (26%) for a broader time period (Feb 1–Sep 23, 2020). However, one source (pesquisa.bvsalud.org) states that "all excess deaths during that period were directly attributed to COVID-19," directly contradicting both the JAMA data and the claim.

**Step 2: What's still lacking**

The main unresolved tension is between the JAMA study's clear numerical data (150,541 of 225,530 excess deaths attributed to COVID, leaving ~33% unattributed) and the contradictory statement from the pesquisa source. However, the JAMA study's numbers are specific, concrete, and come from a peer-reviewed source published in a top medical journal, while the contradicting source makes a vague blanket assertion inconsistent with those same numbers. The mathematical calculation from the JAMA data is straightforward and directly supports the claim's figure of "a third."

**Step 3: Conclusion**

The JAMA study data clearly shows that of 225,530 excess deaths between March 1 and August 1, 2020, only 150,541 (67%) were directly attributed to COVID-19 on death certificates, leaving approximately 33% — roughly a third — not directly attributed to the coronavirus. This directly matches the claim's stated proportion, time frame, and geographic scope. While one source contradicts this, its blanket assertion is inconsistent with the specific JAMA figures. The weight of the evidence supports the claim.

`supported`

The evidence clearly states that Pennsylvania rejected 372,000 *applications* for mail-in ballots, not 372,000 cast mail-in ballots. This occurred during the 2020 general election cycle, with over 90% of rejections being due to duplicate applications. Voters who submitted these duplicate applications could still receive a ballot or vote in person on Election Day.

**Conclusion:** The claim is `refuted`. The recorded evidence explicitly and clearly refutes the claim by demonstrating that the figure of 372,000 refers to rejected ballot applications, not rejected cast ballots.

The search results reference different comments by him about false allegations or sarcastic humor on a radio show, but none contain or support the quoted phrase about his father and rape. The absence of any corroborating evidence from reputable sources or fact-checking organizations indicates the claim lacks factual basis.

The key information still lacking is any authentic, original source for the quote. Without evidence that the statement was actually made, the claim cannot be validated.

Given the complete lack of supporting evidence and the fact that the retrieved information does not contain or imply the quote, the claim is not supported. Therefore, my conclusion is `refuted`.

P.claim: A man who received four ballot applications votes four times in the 2020 election.
P.justification: The claim that a man voted four times in the 2020 election after receiving four ballot applications is refuted by the evidence gathered. According to [Fox29](https://www.fox29.com/news/receiving-multiple-ballot-applications-wont-let-you-vote-more-than-once-heres-why), voters in Illinois could receive multiple ballot applications due to a new state law requiring election officials to mail vote-by-mail applications to registered voters and because outside organizations, including political parties, may also send ballot request forms—however, receiving multiple applications does not permit casting multiple votes. Election systems include safeguards against duplicate voting: as noted by the [North Carolina State Board of Elections](https://www.ncsbe.gov/voting/provisional-voting), pollbook records can flag when a voter has already cast a ballot, triggering a provisional ballot and investigation. The only official investigation referenced in the record involved a [Texas Tribune](https://www.texastribune.org/2020/09/24/texas-gregg-county-voter-fraud/) report about a Gregg County, Texas case from a 2018 primary election—an entirely different incident—where individuals were indicted for fraudulently claiming voters were disabled on mail-in ballot applications, not for using multiple applications to vote repeatedly in the 2020 election.
P.judge_reasoning:
The fact-check examined evidence regarding the mechanisms for receiving multiple ballot applications and the systems in place to detect and prevent multiple voting. The key finding is that while voters can receive multiple applications due to state mailings and outside organizations, election systems are designed to flag and prevent the casting of more than one vote per person, typically through pollbook checks that issue provisional ballots for suspected duplicate voting. However, the recorded evidence does not contain any specific information about the alleged 2020 incident itself.

The critical missing information is any record of an actual investigation, charge, or confirmed instance of a man voting four times in the 2020 election. The evidence provided discusses general procedures (Illinois, North Carolina) and a different case (Texas, 2018), but none of it addresses the specific claim about the 2020 election.

Given the lack of any evidence confirming the specific event described in the claim, and the absence of a reported investigation or outcome, the claim is not supported by the recorded facts. Therefore, the claim is refuted.

`refuted`

P.claim: Most deaths in the 1918 influenza pandemic originated from bacterial pneumonia caused by face masks and that Dr Anthony Fauci, the US government’s top expert in the fight against Covid-19, knew about it.
P.justification: The claim is refuted by scientific and historical consensus: research confirms that secondary bacterial pneumonia was the primary cause of death during the 1918 influenza pandemic, resulting from the virus damaging the respiratory tract and allowing bacterial invasion, not from face mask use. Multiple peer-reviewed studies and public health institutions, such as [The Journal of Infectious Diseases](https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/198/7/962/2192118), [the NIH](https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/bacterial-pneumonia-caused-most-deaths-1918-influenza-pandemic), and [CIDRAP](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/influenza-vaccines/study-bacterial-pneumonia-was-main-killer-1918-flu-pandemic), attribute the deaths to this bacterial complication without linking it to masks. A fringe paper speculating on mask risks lacks empirical evidence, and agencies like the CDC have explicitly denied that masks caused pneumonia ([Daily Herald](https://www.dailyherald.com/20200704/news/facts-matter-pneumonia-not-caused-by-wearing-face-mask/)). The part of the claim involving Dr. Fauci is also unsupported, as his cited research aligns with the bacterial pneumonia finding but does not support the mask theory.
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the key findings are that while secondary bacterial pneumonia was indeed the primary cause of death during the 1918 influenza pandemic, this was a consequence of the viral infection damaging the respiratory tract and enabling bacterial invasion. Multiple reputable sources, including a study co-authored by Dr. Anthony Fauci, confirm this biological mechanism. However, no evidence from the recorded sources establishes any link between the use of face masks and an increased incidence of bacterial pneumonia during that pandemic. In fact, the available information refutes the notion that masks acted as a primary vector for the pathogens and indicates the claim about masks causing deaths is not part of mainstream scientific consensus.

Therefore, the evidence explicitly refutes the claim that most 1918 pandemic deaths were caused by bacterial pneumonia from face masks. The second part of the claim—that Dr. Fauci knew about this—is unsubstantiated, as his documented knowledge, based on his own published research, pertains to bacterial pneumonia as the cause of death, not to a mask-related origin. The evidence clearly contradicts the core causal assertion of the claim.

`refuted`

P.claim: BJP MP Kirron Kher Said "Rape Is A Part Of Indian Culture And It Can't Be Stopped"
P.justification: The claim is false. According to a [Times of India fact-check](https://m.timesofindia.com/times-fact-check/news/fake-alert-bjp-mp-kirron-kher-didnt-say-rape-is-part-of-indian-culture/articleshow/78687624.cms), BJP MP Kirron Kher never made the attributed statement; it originated from a fabricated graphic card traced to a known misinformation source. Her actual words, quoted from a video report, were: "Rapes have been happening for long in India. If we want to stop rapes, the mindset of society towards women needs to be changed. We need to award death penalty to rapists." Her call for the death penalty as a deterrent was deliberately twisted to falsely portray her as saying rape is part of Indian culture. No verified records—such as official parliamentary transcripts, video footage, or credible news reports—exist to support the alleged quote, and [The Logical Indian](https://thelogicalindian.com/tags/kirron-kher) also referred to the statement as unverified "purported" content shared on social media.
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the key finding is that while Kirron Kher is a BJP MP, there is no verified record of her making the exact statement attributed to her. A fact-check article from The Logical Indian identifies the quote as a "purported statement" from social media, and a Times of India fact-check explicitly labels it as fake news, clarifying that her actual words were a call for changing societal mindsets and awarding the death penalty to rapists, which is the opposite of the claim's sentiment.

The evidence is clear and sufficient for a decision; no further investigation is required.

The fact-check explicitly refutes the claim by demonstrating the statement is fabricated and misrepresents Kirron Kher's actual, documented position. Therefore, the claim is `refuted`.

P.claim: A message will be sent to your phone claiming to show that the Covid19 curve is flattening in India, But It will contain a malicious file
P.justification: The fact-check is supported by evidence showing that cybersecurity firms [Kaspersky Lab and Quick Heal](https://www.gao.gov/blog/covid-19-aid-arrives%2C-be-lookout-scams/created) confirmed a malicious file as a SpyNote trojan variant in COVID-19 related messages in October 2020. This campaign was also [documented by India's Cyber Crime Coordination Centre](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmed.2020.00250/created). The malicious messages were distributed via [WhatsApp](https://www.boomlive.in/fast-check/hoax-message-claims-india-is-doing-it-video-will-hack-your-phone-10210) and contained an [APK file](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2019-06/DNR_2019_FINAL_0.pdf/created) designed to compromise device security.
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the documented evidence, the fact-check reveals that in October 2020, a malicious campaign circulated messages, primarily via WhatsApp, claiming to show COVID-19 curve flattening data for India. These messages contained a malicious APK file identified by cybersecurity firms (Kaspersky Lab and Quick Heal) as a SpyNote trojan variant designed to compromise device security. This campaign was recognized by Indian cybercrime authorities and cybersecurity agencies, confirming its existence as a time-bound, organized threat.

The evidence is clear and comprehensive: it confirms the message's content, the presence of a malicious file, the distribution channel, and the intent of the payload. No further investigation is required, as the findings directly align with all aspects of the claim.

Therefore, the claim is substantiated by the recorded evidence. `supported`

Given the explicit statements from what appears to be an official Notre Dame source that Barrett "achieved no class rank," the claim that she "graduated at the top of her class" is contradicted. While she received a prestigious academic honor, the evidence directly refutes the specific claim of holding an official top class rank. Therefore, the decision is `refuted`.

P.claim: Saved by the Bell actor, Dustin Diamond died in a prison riot.
P.justification: The claim is refuted as Dustin Diamond died from stage 4 small cell carcinoma (lung cancer) on February 1, 2021, not from injuries sustained in a prison riot. Although briefly incarcerated in 2015, he was released before his death, and there are no credible official reports or reliable news accounts linking his passing to any prison disturbance. The coroner's report and family details confirm his death was from natural causes, with his remains cremated according to his wishes. Sources explicitly debunking the riot narrative include [IMDB](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0224616/trivia/) and a [Medium article](https://medium.com/whither-news/a-call-for-cooperation-against-fake-news-d7d94bb6e0d4/created) identifying the riot story as misinformation.
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the fact-check evidence, the key findings are that Dustin Diamond was indeed a *Saved by the Bell* actor who died on February 1, 2021. The recorded cause of death, as supported by credible sources like IMDB trivia, was stage 4 small cell carcinoma (lung cancer). The only sources claiming a death in a prison riot are from unreliable articles explicitly framed as examples of fake news or misinformation, and no credible news reports, official reports, or family statements corroborate the prison riot narrative.

The information needed to finalize the fact-check is already complete, as the evidence clearly and credibly contradicts the claim's assertion about the cause of death.

Therefore, the claim that Dustin Diamond died in a prison riot is false and is directly refuted by the available evidence. The conclusion is `refuted`.

Medical bodies, such as the [New Zealand College of Midwives](https://www.midwife.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/Abortion-Act-summary_JUNE2020.pdf), confirm permitted methods like medication abortion using mifepristone and misoprostol. However, there is no evidence within the Act's text, parliamentary debate, or medical documentation that any of these allowed methods are characterised or defined as "controversial"; the term is a subjective political or social opinion, not a factual description of the law's provisions. Therefore, the claim is refuted.
P.judge_reasoning:
### Step 1: Summary of Key Insights
The fact-check confirms that the New Zealand Abortion Legislation Act 2020 legalizes abortion under specific conditions, allowing it up to 20 weeks without restriction and with assessment thereafter. Medical sources list permitted methods (e.g., mifepristone and misoprostol), but none of the retrieved evidence—from the Act's text, official summaries, or medical guidelines—characterizes any allowed method as "controversial." The term appears to be an external or political opinion, not a factual description embedded in the law.

### Step 2: Missing Information
To definitively support the claim, we would need evidence showing that the Act itself, authoritative medical bodies, or widely recognized public discourse in New Zealand explicitly labels specific abortion methods permitted under the law as "controversial." No such evidence was found.

### Step 3: Conclusion
Based solely on the recorded evidence, the claim is not supported because while the Act permits certain abortion procedures, no source indicates these are deemed "controversial" by the law or its official interpreters; the characterization is subjective. Therefore, the final decision is `refuted`.

The claim thus distorts the nature and target of his remarks, leading to a **REFUTED** verdict.
P.judge_reasoning:

However, the provided sources only detail Gascon's position and the military engagement; they do not contain any statement from Gascon regarding this specific incident, nor do they characterize the operation as a "surprise military attack" or record him calling it a "violation of human rights."

The key missing information is any direct evidence linking Chairman Gascon to the quoted reaction described in the claim. To finalize the fact-check, we would need a source documenting his specific statement or commentary about this military operation.

Therefore, based solely on the recorded evidence which provides no support for the specific statement attributed to Chito Gascon, the claim is `refuted`.

P.justification: A federal lawsuit accusing Donald Trump of sexually assaulting a 13-year-old was filed in Manhattan in 2016 under the pseudonym "Katie Johnson," but it was **voluntarily dismissed** by the plaintiff in November 2016 [Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/news/2016/06/23/donald-trump-rape-lawsuit/). Therefore, the claim that he "currently faces" such a case is refuted, as the lawsuit is inactive.

The fact-check found that while a federal lawsuit was filed in 2016 under the pseudonym "Katie Johnson" accusing Donald Trump of sexually assaulting a 13-year-old, it was voluntarily dismissed in November 2016. A related court filing was noted in October 2020, but the evidence does not indicate this constituted a new, active case. The sources provided no corroboration of the allegations and noted the absence of any official criminal investigation.

The key missing information is any evidence that a court case concerning these specific allegations is currently active or pending. The recorded evidence points only to past, concluded legal actions.

Based on the recorded evidence, the claim that Donald Trump *currently* faces a court case for this allegation is not supported. The lawsuit referenced was dismissed years ago, and there is no indication from the sources that it has been revived or is ongoing. Therefore, the claim is refuted.

`refuted`

Apple confirmed during its iPhone 12 launch event that it would remove both the EarPods and the charging adapter from the retail box for all iPhone 12 models, citing environmental reasons such as reducing carbon emissions ([Daily Mail](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/sciencetech/article-8840611/Apple-customers-outraged-learning-799-iPhone-12-NOT-include-charger-EarPods.html)). While some unreliable sources (e.g., a Microsoft support page and a retailer listing) contradict this, the credible evidence from Apple and established tech reviewers is consistent and definitive.

No further information is needed, as the primary sources provide a clear and direct answer.

Conclusion: The claim that "The iPhone 12 won’t come with earphones and a charging adapter" is directly confirmed by Apple's official announcement and supported by independent verification from tech media. Therefore, the decision is `supported`.

P.claim: New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020) does not make it a legal requirement that babies born alive after an abortion are given medical support.

During the legislative process, a specific amendment (by MP Simon O'Connor) that would have created such a legal duty was explicitly debated and rejected by Parliament, confirming that the Act's silence on this matter is intentional.

The evidence is clear and comprehensive regarding the Act's provisions and the legislative intent behind their omission, so no further information is required to finalize the check.

`supported`

This means he had nominated **two out of nine justices**, not a "full third." His third nominee, Amy Coney Barrett, was announced in September 2020 but had not been confirmed or seated by the specified date.

P.claim: Amy Coney Barrett's nomination to the Supreme Court would be confirmed in October 2020, by a Senate majority that represents 15 million fewer people than the minority party.
P.justification: While Amy Coney Barrett was indeed confirmed to the Supreme Court on October 26, 2020, the specific figure that the confirming majority represented "15 million fewer people" than the minority is inaccurate. The standard method for calculating population representation assigns each senator the full population of their state, and using this approach, the stated disparity does not hold. The verdict is **REFUTED**.

However, the specific population disparity claim is directly contradicted by the evidence. A major news outlet (Vox) reported that the confirming senators represented 161.9 million people, and another source explicitly states that the "15 million fewer" figure misapplies voting-eligible population data, indicating it is not a valid comparison of total state populations.

The claim contains a factual assertion about the population represented by the Senate majority that is explicitly refuted by the recorded evidence. Therefore, the claim is not supported.

P.claim: President Trump said Anthony Fauci said, “This is not a threat. This is not a problem. Don’t worry about it.” when talking about the pandemic
P.justification: The claim is **REFUTED** because Dr. Anthony Fauci never made the exact statement attributed to him. According to [FactCheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2020/04/trump-misquotes-fauci-on-coronavirus-threat/), during a [February 29, 2020, interview on NBC's "Today" show](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/politics-news/fauci-says-coronavirus-outbreak-keeps-me-night-n1194351/created), Fauci actually said, "Right now, at this moment, there's no need to change anything that you're doing on a day-by-day basis. Right now the risk is still low, but this could change," while warning of a potential "major outbreak." While Trump did reference Fauci's remarks on [April 28, 2020](https://www.factcheck.org/2020/04/trump-misquotes-fauci-on-coronavirus-threat/), he paraphrased them differently, saying Fauci was saying "this is no problem. This is going to blow over"—which was itself a mischaracterization. Fauci later [clarified to CNN](https://www.statesman.com/story/news/politics/elections/2020/10/12/fact-check-did-dr-anthony-fauci-praise-trumprsquos-coronavirus-response/42746661/) that his original comments were "taken out of context" and were directed at the broader federal public health response, not used as an endorsement of any individual. No official transcript, audio, or video recording documents Fauci ever saying the three-part quote in the claim.
P.judge_reasoning:
### Step 1: Summary of Key Insights
The fact-check reveals that Dr. Anthony Fauci never made a public or recorded statement with the exact words "This is not a threat. This is not a problem. Don't worry about it." in reference to the COVID-19 pandemic. Instead, on February 29, 2020, during an NBC "Today" show interview, Fauci stated that the risk was "still low" but "could change," while warning of a potential outbreak. President Donald Trump, in an April 28, 2020, press briefing, attributed a similar but not identical statement to Fauci, paraphrasing him as saying "this is no problem. This is going to blow over," a characterization later clarified by Fauci as taken out of context. No evidence supports that either Trump or Fauci used the precise three-part phrase claimed.

### Step 2: Lack of Information (Not Applicable)
The evidence is clear and sufficient to finalize the fact-check; no additional information is needed.

### Step 3: Conclusion
Based on the fact-check, the claim that President Trump said Anthony Fauci said the exact quote "This is not a threat. This is not a problem. Don't worry about it." is explicitly refuted by the recorded evidence, as neither the original statement by Fauci nor its attribution by Trump matches this precise wording. `refuted`

P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the key findings are that multiple sources, including an official government transcript and reputable news outlets, confirm that during her 2020 Supreme Court confirmation hearing, Amy Coney Barrett stated she was not using notes because she has seven kids and is used to "stupid questions." The remark is consistently reported as a humorous, self-deprecating analogy made in a formal setting.

The evidence is clear and consistent, leaving no significant gaps that require further investigation to verify the core elements of the claim.

Therefore, the claim is directly supported by the documented statements from the hearing. `supported`

P.claim: CNN announces on social media that President Donald Trump dies from COVID-19.
P.justification: The claim that CNN announced on social media that President Donald Trump died from COVID-19 is **refuted**. An investigation found that CNN did not publish any such announcement on its verified social media accounts. While some search snippets referenced an Instagram post, the linked [AP News article](https://apnews.com/article/virus-outbreak-donald-trump-elections-melania-trump-michael-pence-f6ba3a16ab9b74b161a3a7211248e97e) actually reports on Trump recovering and returning to the campaign trail after his October 2020 COVID-19 diagnosis. There were no official medical, White House, or government statements confirming his death, as he did not die from the illness.
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the fact-check reveals significant contradictions. While several answers (Q2, Q3, Q5, Q6) reference an alleged CNN Instagram post on October 13, 2020, and even claim official White House confirmation of death, these assertions are directly and explicitly contradicted by other parts of the record (Q1, Q7). The primary source cited (an AP News article) is used both to support and refute the claim, indicating the evidence is incoherent and unreliable. Furthermore, the factual reality—that Donald Trump contracted COVID-19 in 2020 but survived—is a matter of common public knowledge not disputed by the credible evidence in the record.

To finalize the fact-check, we are lacking clear, consistent, and credible evidence. There is no reliable primary source (e.g., a direct link to a CNN social media post) confirming the announcement, and the supposed official confirmations of death are refuted by other evidence within the same record. The evidence is too contradictory to establish the claim as true.

The claim states that CNN officially announced Donald Trump's death from COVID-19 on social media. The recorded evidence is internally inconsistent and, on the whole, more strongly indicates the announcement did not happen, as key answers explicitly refute it and the foundational fact—that Trump is alive—contradicts the claim's premise. Therefore, the claim is not supported by the evidence.

`refuted`

P.claim: 18-year-old man was recently killed by Trinamool Congress workers in West Bengal for supporting BJP
P.justification: The fact-check concludes the claim is refuted due to conflicting and unverified information. While [The Statesman](https://www.thestatesman.com/india/fresh-arrests-made-bjp-supporter-murder-case-1502685242.html) reported that witnesses and a confession implicated TMC workers, official statements from [local police](https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/body-of-another-bjp-worker-found-hanging-from-pole-in-bengal/story-tlZTzcLOtp1zrgPGOMN7yH.html) suggested the death was a suicide or the result of personal enmity, not a political killing. Furthermore, the Trinamool Congress issued no statement, and key sources like the cited [Rediff slideshow](https://www.rediff.com/news/slide-show/slide-show-1-purulia-arms-case-davy-cant-be-extradited/20110630.htm) were found to be about unrelated topics, undermining the evidence provided.
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the fact-check confirms that an 18-year-old BJP supporter was killed in West Bengal in late September/October 2020, with multiple eyewitnesses and a TMC member's confession implicating Trinamool Congress workers in the attack. However, key uncertainties and contradictions remain: the victim's identity and precise circumstances are not detailed, the sources provided are questionable or point to unrelated content, and the police investigation initially indicated the death was a suicide possibly due to personal enmity, contradicting the claim's direct attribution to political violence.

The information still lacking to finalize this fact-check includes: credible, detailed reports from major news outlets (the cited *Statesman* and *Rediff* links are non-functional or point to unrelated pages), the official police findings and arrest records for this specific case, and any formal statements from the TMC denying or addressing the specific allegation. The motive for the killing, while implied by the claim, is not conclusively established by the evidence provided.

Given the significant gaps in source reliability and the direct contradiction from a police official who suggested suicide and personal enmity rather than a political killing, the collected evidence does not robustly support the claim as presented. Therefore, the claim is not adequately supported by the recorded findings.

`refuted`

P.claim: Fact check: Harris' statement on Lincoln's Supreme Court nomination misses key details
P.justification: Kamala Harris's statement that Abraham Lincoln refrained from filling a Supreme Court vacancy close to his 1864 reelection is factually correct, as [historical records confirm](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/lincoln-1864-supreme-court/) he did not nominate a justice during that period, a point the fact-check supports. However, the verdict of "SUPPORTED" is qualified because her account [omits key contextual details](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/10/13/fact-check-harris-lesson-lincoln-supreme-court-nom-lacks-detail/5943183002/): Congress was in recess until December 5, 1864, which prevented immediate confirmation, and Lincoln's delay was also a strategic [political calculation](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/lincoln-1864-supreme-court/) to secure support from key figures like Salmon P. Chase for his post-war agenda.
P.judge_reasoning:
**Step 1: Summary of Key Insights from Fact-Check**  
The fact-check confirms that Kamala Harris’s core claim—that Abraham Lincoln, despite having his party in charge of the White House and Senate, chose not to nominate a Supreme Court justice close to his 1864 re-election—is factually accurate. However, the evidence reveals significant omissions in her statement: the vacancy arose after Chief Justice Roger B. Taney’s death on October 12, 1864, and the Senate was in recess until December, making immediate confirmation impossible; Lincoln’s delay was also a calculated political move to secure support from rivals like Salmon P. Chase, whom he later nominated. These details complicate Harris’s narrative of principled restraint.

**Step 2: Missing Information**  
No further investigation is required; the retrieved evidence is clear and sufficient for a decision. The sources explicitly state Harris’s omission of "key details" (e.g., recess, political strategy) while affirming the basic factual accuracy of her statement.

**Step 3: Conclusion**  
Based on the evidence, Harris’s statement omitted contextual details—such as the Senate recess and Lincoln’s political motivations—which the fact-check identifies as key. The headline’s claim that her statement "misses key details" is directly supported by the fact-check’s findings, which highlight these omissions without disputing the core historical fact. Therefore, the claim is `supported`.

P.claim: Daughters of President Muhammadu Buhari and Vice President Yemi Osinbajo brought about the dissolution of Special Anti-Robbery Squad (SARS).
P.justification: The claim that the daughters of Nigeria's President and Vice President "brought about" the dissolution of SARS is **refuted**. While Zahra Buhari posted a solidarity image on Instagram and [Kiki Osinbajo reportedly lobbied her father](https://www.bbc.com/pidgin/tori-47153979/created), these were minor social media and personal actions, not the driving force behind SARS's dissolution. The widely recognized cause was the massive, youth-led [#EndSARS protest movement](https://www.nme.com/news/music/wizkid-is-leading-mass-protests-against-nigerian-police-brutality-in-london-2779949) in October 2020, which generated intense domestic and international pressure—including from organizations like Amnesty International—prompting the [Inspector General of Police to announce SARS's dissolution on October 11, 2020](https://citinewsroom.com/2020/10/endsars-nigerias-notorious-police-unit-dissolved-after-citizens-protests/). No credible, independently verified official statement from the Nigerian Presidency or Vice Presidency has been identified that attributes the decision to the daughters' advocacy; the [AFP Fact Check page](https://factcheck.afp.com/busting-coronavirus-myths/created) frequently cited as a source for this assertion is itself a fact-check debunking the claim rather than confirming it.
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the fact-check record, the evidence shows that while the daughters of both leaders made supportive social media posts regarding the #EndSARS movement and one report suggests the Vice President's daughter lobbied her father, the overwhelming and directly cited reason for the dissolution of SARS was the massive nationwide and international #EndSARS protests. There is no credible evidence of an official government statement or announcement attributing the decision specifically to the daughters' actions; in fact, the most authoritative sources, including the Inspector General of Police's announcement and reports from outlets like NME, credit the collective protest movement and international pressure.

The information still lacking is a direct, verifiable statement from an official Nigerian government source (such as from the Presidency, Vice Presidency, or the Police) that explicitly identifies the daughters' advocacy as the causal reason for SARS's dissolution, rather than the protests. The single source that appears to make this claim is itself a fact-check article, casting doubt on its reliability as independent verification.

Therefore, based on the recorded evidence, the claim that the daughters "brought about the dissolution" is not sufficiently supported. The documented catalyst for the government's action was the widespread public protest movement, not the actions of the two individuals mentioned. The claim is `refuted`.

P.claim: The Median White Household Wealth In The US Is 81 Times that of The Black Median Household Wealth
P.justification: The fact-check determined that the claimed 81:1 ratio is not supported by the most authoritative data; the U.S. Federal Reserve's 2019 Survey of Consumer Finances reports a ratio of approximately [8:1](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/disparities-in-wealth-by-race-and-ethnicity-in-the-2019-survey-of-consumer-finances-accessible-20200928.htm). While a separate 2020 [source](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/the-racial-wealth-gap/) does state an 81:1 ratio, it does not align with the Federal Reserve's survey figures, and other major analyses, such as a [Pew Research Center report](https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2011/07/26/wealth-gaps-rise-to-record-highs-between-whites-blacks-hispanics/) using 2009 Census data, found a lower ratio of 20:1. Therefore, the claim significantly overstates the wealth disparity as measured by primary sources.
P.judge_reasoning:
The fact-check reveals a significant discrepancy between the claimed 81:1 ratio and the data from the most authoritative source, the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF). The 2019 SCF explicitly states the ratio of median white to median Black household wealth is approximately 8 to 1 ($188,200 vs. $24,100). While one non-authoritative source cites an 81:1 ratio for 2020, this is an outlier and is not supported by the Federal Reserve's own published data, which is the benchmark for such statistics. Other major, credible surveys like Pew Research Center have also reported much lower ratios (e.g., 20:1 for 2009).

The evidence from the authoritative source is clear and does not support the claim. No further investigation is needed to finalize the fact-check. The recorded data directly and explicitly refutes the specific 81:1 ratio.

`refuted`

**Source:** [Bhaskar fact-check (Hindi)](https://www.bhaskar.com/no-fake-news/news/rahul-gandhi-ranks-7th-in-most-educated-leaders-in-the-worlds-reality-check-01447173.html)

Multiple fact-checking investigations, including a detailed report from Dainik Bhaskar, confirm that Forbes has never published any ranking or list of the world's most educated leaders. The evidence explicitly states that no such list was found on Forbes' website or anywhere else, and the claim originates from unverified social media posts. There are no credible sources, including Forbes itself, that support the existence of this ranking or Rahul Gandhi's placement in it.

The evidence is clear and unambiguous: the claim directly states that Forbes published a specific list, which the records prove never existed. Therefore, no further investigation is needed to verify the specifics of a non-existent list.

The fact-check findings explicitly and clearly refute the claim. Forbes has never published the described list of educated leaders, so it is impossible for Rahul Gandhi to have been ranked seventh in it. The claim is false.

`refuted`

P.claim: Donald Trump is facing a court case for raping a teen in 1994
P.justification: A civil lawsuit was filed by an anonymous plaintiff ("Jane Doe") alleging that Donald Trump raped her in 1994 when she was 13, at parties hosted by Jeffrey Epstein, but the case was [voluntarily dismissed in November 2016](https://www.inquisitr.com/3692292/donald-trump-rape-accuser-katie-johnson-lied-she-was-not-sexually-assaulted-by-trump-at-age-13-report) before the presidential election and is no longer an active court case. Since the claim states Trump "is facing a court case," but no such active case exists, the verdict is **REFUTED**.
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the fact-check, the key findings are that a civil lawsuit making the alleged accusation was filed but was voluntarily dismissed in November 2016 and is no longer an active or pending case. Furthermore, one source indicates the story was "completely fabricated" with no corroboration.

The evidence is clear and sufficient for a conclusion. The claim that Donald Trump "is facing a court case" for the alleged crime is factually inaccurate, as the referenced lawsuit was dismissed and is not a current legal proceeding.

The fact-check explicitly refutes the claim's central assertion of an ongoing or pending court case. Therefore, the decision is `refuted`.

P.claim: Joe Biden said “You know, we have to come together. That’s why I’m running. I’m running as a proud Democrat for the Senate. So vote! Vote!”
P.justification: The fact-check concludes that the claim is **REFUTED** because the exact quote is not verbatim in any reliable source. While a similar statement was made by Joe Biden on October 6, 2020, during his Gettysburg speech, the context shows it was part of his presidential campaign, not a Senate race, and appears to be a verbal slip. The original speech can be verified via [C-SPAN](https://www.c-span.org/) and [ABC News](https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/full-text-joe-bidens-2020-democratic-national-convention/story?id=72513129), which document the presidential context and surrounding remarks.
P.judge_reasoning:
The fact-check reveals that while Joe Biden did utter the phrase "I'm running as a proud Democrat for the Senate" during a speech, the exact quote in the claim is not verbatim, and the context is significantly misrepresented. The verified source shows this statement was made on October 6, 2020, during his Gettysburg speech as a presidential candidate, not on January 5, 2024, and it is widely considered a gaffe. The claim's additional phrases ("You know, we have to come together... So vote! Vote!") and the specified date are not supported by the evidence.

The key missing information is any evidence that the statement was made on January 5, 2024, or that the full, exact quote as presented in the claim exists in any primary source. The available evidence directly contradicts the claim's date and shows the quote is a partial and altered version of a real statement.

Based on the recorded evidence, the claim is inaccurate in its attribution of the date and the exact wording. The core statement exists but is taken out of its correct context and time, making the overall claim false. Therefore, the decision is `refuted`.

P.claim: NASA always receives blessings from the Pope and that God’s permission must be sought before a space mission.
P.justification: The claim is entirely without basis: [NASA](https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/2014/03/02/astronaut-faith-outer-space-mars/5946763/) has never had any official policy, guideline, or regulation requiring a blessing from the Pope or permission from God before launching a mission, nor does any [U.S. federal law or regulation](https://www.spacescience.org/education/extra/saturn_educator_guide/Chapters/questions_answers_lr.pdf) mandate such religious approval. [Historical records and official NASA communications](https://earthzine.org/nasas-hurricane-webpage-a-resource-for-worldwide-tropical-cyclones-2/) contain no evidence that the agency ever requested or received papal blessings for any of its major missions. While [Pope Benedict XVI spoke with astronauts aboard the ISS in 2011](https://www.space.com/11741-pope-benedict-xvi-calls-astronauts-space-station-sts134.html), this was a gesture of goodwill, not an exercise of authority over NASA's operations, and neither the Vatican nor any Pope has ever publicly claimed to grant NASA permission for its missions. NASA's actual [approval processes](https://lws.larc.nasa.gov/pdf_files/13%20nasa-std-1006.pdf) are entirely secular, focusing on technical, operational, and safety requirements with no religious component. While [Roscosmos has a tradition of having Russian Orthodox priests bless Soyuz rockets](https://time.com/3759467/rocket-blessing-soyuz/), this practice is unrelated to NASA and involves the Russian Orthodox Church, not the Pope. There is [no evidence of any formal chain of communication or documentation between NASA and the Holy See](https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/2014/03/02/astronaut-faith-outer-space-mars/5946763/), as NASA operates as a secular U.S. government agency; references to a supposed "binding 1964 accord" are unsubstantiated misinformation.
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded fact-check, the key evidence consistently and directly refutes the claim. The investigation found no official NASA policy, U.S. law, or historical record requiring a blessing from the Pope or permission from God for space missions. NASA's approval processes are documented as secular, focusing on technical and safety protocols. Furthermore, the Vatican has engaged in goodwill interactions with astronauts but has never asserted any authority over NASA's operations. While another space agency (Roscosmos) has its own religious blessing tradition, no such practice is linked to NASA.

No significant information gaps remain; the retrieved evidence clearly addresses and disproves both components of the claim.

Therefore, the conclusion is that the knowledge from the fact-check explicitly refutes the claim. `refuted`

P.claim: Most Arab citizens support normalization with Israel.
P.justification: The claim that "most Arab citizens support normalization with Israel" is **refuted** by the available polling evidence. While a 2020 poll by the [Israel Democracy Institute](https://adst.org/OH%20TOCs/White-Wayne.pdf/created) surveyed 1,200 Arab citizens of Israel with a ±2.8% margin of error, it only captured the views of one specific subgroup rather than Arab citizens broadly. In contrast, a far more comprehensive survey conducted by the [Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies (ACRPS)](https://www.trtworld.com/magazine/arab-majorities-overwhelmingly-oppose-any-normalisation-with-israel-40385) across 13 Arab countries between November 2019 and September 2020 found that an overwhelming majority (88%) of Arabs disapprove of recognition of Israel by their home countries, with only 6% accepting formal diplomatic recognition. Opposition was exceptionally high in countries such as Algeria (99%), Lebanon (94%), Tunisia (93%), and Jordan (93%), and even in Gulf states like Qatar and Kuwait (nearly 90% rejection) and Saudi Arabia (65% rejection). This broader and more representative evidence strongly contradicts the claim.
P.judge_reasoning:
**Summary of Key Insights:**  
The fact-check examined two primary polling sources on Arab public opinion regarding normalization with Israel. A 2020 poll by the Israel Democracy Institute surveyed 1,200 Arab citizens of Israel and found support for normalization. However, a broader survey conducted by the Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies (ACRPS) across 13 Arab countries between late 2019 and 2020 found that 88% of respondents opposed recognition of Israel by their home countries, with opposition ranging from 65% to 99% across different nations.

**Missing Information:**  
No further information is needed, as the available evidence clearly addresses the claim.

**Conclusion:**  
Based on the recorded evidence, the ACRPS poll—which represents a wide cross-section of Arab public opinion across multiple countries—explicitly refutes the claim that most Arab citizens support normalization with Israel, showing instead that an overwhelming majority oppose it. Therefore, the claim is `refuted`.

P.claim: The PHE has began to combine Covid-19 and influenza statistics to make the numbers look worse.
P.justification: The fact-check finds no evidence that Public Health England (PHE) officially combined COVID-19 and influenza statistics; their published reports consistently presented separate data for each disease. While internal documents suggested the idea was considered, there is no confirmation it was implemented, and the stated purpose was not to inflate numbers. The practice of integrated respiratory surveillance is used by other agencies for legitimate public health monitoring, but PHE's actual reporting did not merge the statistics as claimed.
P.judge_reasoning:
Based on the recorded evidence, the fact-check found no confirmation that Public Health England (PHE) officially combined COVID-19 and influenza statistics into a single reporting category. While internal documents and a leaked draft press release suggested the idea was considered to "present a more alarming picture," official PHE reports consistently presented separate surveillance data for both diseases. Furthermore, other public health agencies combine respiratory data for legitimate epidemiological reasons, and there is no evidence from PHE statements that the purpose was to inflate COVID-19 numbers.

The key missing information is verifiable proof that PHE actually implemented a policy of combining these statistics, as opposed to merely discussing it internally. The available evidence does not show a change in PHE's official reporting practices.

Therefore, the claim that PHE began combining COVID-19 and influenza statistics to make the numbers look worse is not supported by the evidence. The fact-check indicates that while the idea was considered, it was not officially implemented, and the intent alleged in the claim is not substantiated. `refuted`

P.claim: A law called The Flora and Fauna Act classified aboriginal people as animals until Australian voters overturned it in the 1960s.
P.justification: The claim is refuted because there was never an Australian law officially titled "The Flora and Fauna Act" that classified Aboriginal people as fauna ([audit.vic.gov.au](https://www.audit.vic.gov.au/report/administration-flora-and-fauna-guarantee-act-1988/?section=)); this is a widespread urban myth with no basis in legislative history ([SBS](https://www.sbs.com.au/nitv/article/shareena-clanton-is-like-many-of-us-a-victim-of-the-flora-and-fauna-act-myth/m40dgtgah)). The 1967 referendum did not repeal such an act; instead, it amended the Australian Constitution to allow the federal government to make laws for Aboriginal people and include them in population counts ([University of Queensland](https://web.library.uq.edu.au/blog/2017/05/1967-referendum)).
P.judge_reasoning:
**Summary of Key Insights:**  
The recorded evidence overwhelmingly shows that no Australian legislation was ever officially titled "The Flora and Fauna Act." While one source suggests such a law classified Aboriginal people as fauna, multiple authoritative sources—including SBS and Wikipedia—explicitly identify this claim as a persistent urban myth with no basis in legislative history. The 1967 referendum did occur and was a significant constitutional change regarding Aboriginal rights, but it amended the Constitution to include Aboriginal people in population counts and grant the federal government legislative power over them; it did not repeal any so-called "Flora and Fauna Act" because such an act never existed.

**Missing Information:**  
No further investigation is required, as the evidence is clear and consistent in refuting the claim’s foundational assertions.

**Conclusion:**  
Based on the fact-check, the claim that "A law called The Flora and Fauna Act classified aboriginal people as animals until Australian voters overturned it in the 1960s" is not supported by historical records. The evidence indicates the "Flora and Fauna Act" is a myth, and the 1967 referendum did not address or overturn such a law. Therefore, the claim is `refuted`.

PM.claim: In a letter to Steve Jobs, Sean Connery refused to appear in an apple commercial.
PM.justification: The widely circulated letter in which Sean Connery supposedly refused to appear in an Apple commercial has been identified as a fabrication originating from the satirical website [Scoopertino](https://www.cnet.com/culture/fake-sean-connery-letter-to-steve-jobs-goes-viral/). No historian, archivist, or biographer of either Sean Connery or Steve Jobs has authenticated the existence of such correspondence ([Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/james-bond-sean-connery-steve-jobs-apple-letter-2011-6)), and there is no documented evidence that the letter is genuine. While Apple did run campaigns seeking major film stars in the 1990s ([Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/apple-history-through-advertising-40-years-anniversary-2016-3)) and Steve Jobs was known for his hands-on involvement in advertising ([thisisnotadvertising](https://thisisnotadvertising.wordpress.com/2011/09/05/apple-think-different/)), the specific claim about Connery's letter rests entirely on a debunked piece of satirical content, leading to the verdict of **REFUTED**.
PM.judge_reasoning:
Based on the fact-check, the evidence strongly indicates that the alleged letter from Sean Connery to Steve Jobs refusing an Apple commercial is fabricated. Reputable sources identify the letter as originating from the satirical website Scoopertino, and no authentication by historians or biographers exists. While some marketing websites cite the letter as real, they lack credibility compared to sources like CNET and Business Insider that confirm its inauthenticity. The reasoner's absence of memory for such a notable event, involving two widely recognized figures, further supports this conclusion. No additional investigation is needed.

The claim is refuted because the evidence explicitly contradicts its validity.

`refuted`

PM.claim: Trump Administration claimed songwriter Billie Eilish Is Destroying Our Country In Leaked Documents
PM.justification: The fact-check confirms that leaked internal documents from the Trump Administration’s Department of Health and Human Services did exist as part of a strategy for a $250 million pandemic advertising campaign. These documents explicitly mentioned singer [Billie Eilish by name](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/leaked-trump-admin-document-describes-191559664.html), stating she was "not a Trump supporter" and was "destroying our country and everything we care about." The statement was part of a larger strategic assessment by [HHS officials](https://money.yahoo.com/leaked-trump-admin-document-describes-191559664.html) to exclude certain celebrities from the campaign based on perceived political alignment. While initially reported by the Washington Post, a later correction clarified the documents were a mischaracterization of an internal celebrity screening list, not direct statements from officials ([New York Post via archive](https://web.archive.org/web/20201101145631/https://nypost.com/2020/10/30/washington-post-wrongly-claims-trump-officials-criticized-billie-eilish/)). The documents were not disputed as inauthentic, but the claim’s framing as an official public assertion is refuted.
PM.judge_reasoning:
Based on the fact-check record, the key findings are as follows: There is agreement that leaked documents related to the Trump Administration exist and that the phrase "destroying our country" is attributed to Billie Eilish within them, presented as part of a strategic evaluation for a public health campaign. However, several conflicts arise between the document store and the memory-only reasoner regarding the explicit mention of Eilish by name, the exact phrasing, the document's nature, and the leaking outlet. PM.claim: Someone who couldn't afford health care under Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act gets penalized $10,000
PM.justification: The claim is **REFUTED** because the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate penalty was always capped at either a flat amount or a percentage of income, whichever was greater, and was legally limited to the national average premium for a Bronze-level health plan. Official documentation and analyses from sources like the [Congressional Budget Office](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/43628) show the maximum penalty per person was $695 or 2.5% of income by 2016, and [penalty calculators](https://www.kff.org/interactive/penalty-calculator/) estimate the cap at approximately $3,816 for a single individual in 2018—substantially below $10,000. No official reports show any individual was ever assessed a $10,000 penalty.
PM.judge_reasoning:
**Summary of Key Insights:** The Affordable Care Act did include an individual mandate requiring most people to have health insurance or pay a penalty, officially called the Individual Shared Responsibility Payment. The penalty was calculated based on income or a flat amount, with a legal cap tied to the average cost of a bronze-level marketplace plan. Crucially, the ACA also provided an affordability exemption for individuals whose insurance cost exceeded a certain percentage of their household income (around 8%), meaning those who genuinely could not afford coverage were not subject to the penalty. Conflicts in the record regarding the maximum penalty amount were resolved in favor of the reasoner's recall (supported by other evidence) that the penalty was always capped below $10,000—specifically at the average bronze plan premium, which was estimated at a few thousand dollars during the mandate's enforcement years.

**Missing Information:** No further investigation is required. The evidence clearly shows the penalty amount and the existence of the affordability exemption.

**Conclusion:** The claim that someone who couldn't afford health care under the ACA would be penalized $10,000 is incorrect. The ACA's penalty for non-compliance was capped at the average cost of a bronze plan, which was well below $10,000 during the years the mandate was in effect. More importantly, the law explicitly exempted individuals who could not afford insurance based on a percentage of their income. Therefore, the claim is clearly false. `refuted`

However, the historical evidence reveals that the vacancy on the Court (from Chief Justice Roger B. Taney's death) arose in October 1864, during the presidential campaign, and Lincoln nominated Salmon P. Chase only after winning re-election in November 1864. This indicates the delay was due to the timeline of the vacancy and the election, not a voluntary choice by Lincoln to postpone the nomination for the principle Harris describes, which makes her framing misleading.

The evidence is clear and sufficient to evaluate the claim about the fact-check's conclusion, as it identifies the specific omissions (the post-election timing and context of the nomination) that constitute the "key details" Harris missed.

M.claim: A law called The Flora and Fauna Act classified aboriginal people as animals until Australian voters overturned it in the 1960s.
M.justification: No law officially titled "The Flora and Fauna Act" ever existed in Australian federal or state legislation, and no Australian law ever explicitly classified Aboriginal Australians as "flora" or "fauna" — this is a [widespread myth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_referendum,_1967) with no basis in legislative history. Before 1967, Aboriginal Australians were governed by constitutional provisions such as [Section 127](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_127_of_the_Constitution_of_Australia) (excluding them from population counts) and [Section 51(xxvi)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_51(xxvi)_of_the_Constitution_of_Australia) (limiting Commonwealth legislative power), as well as various state-level Aboriginal Protection Acts that designated them as wards of the state. The [1967 referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Australian_referendum_(Aboriginals)) amended these constitutional provisions to allow the Commonwealth to make laws for Aboriginal people and to include them in the national census, but it did not repeal or modify any nonexistent "Flora and Fauna Act." No primary historical records or legal documents support the existence of such an act.
M.judge_reasoning: Based on the fact-check, the recorded evidence consistently indicates that there is no record of any Australian federal or state legislation officially titled "The Flora and Fauna Act," and no law explicitly classified Aboriginal Australians as "flora" or "fauna" in its text. The 1967 referendum addressed constitutional changes to include Aboriginal people in federal legislation and the census, but it did not repeal or modify any such act, as none existed. Therefore, the claim is a widespread myth with no basis in legal or historical records, leading to the conclusion that it is `refuted`.
